metadata.title: Using process data to understand adults’ problem-solving behaviour in the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The analysis uses PIAAC Survey of Adult Skills process data linked to respondents’ cognitive and background information, restricted to the PS2 PSTRE item cluster in five countries. The paper reports sample sizes by routing path (LIT-PS2, NUM-PS2, PS1-PS2) and excludes respondents with at least one nonresponse action-sequence pattern, but it does not describe the application of PIAAC complex survey weights or replicate weights in the LCS-based indicators. Because the study focuses on sequence-mining-derived similarity/consistency/efficiency indicators and group comparisons (e.g., ANOVA/t-tests), the manuscript does not provide a weight variable name to apply for population-representative inference. Analysts using the PIAAC microdata should consult the PIAAC technical documentation for the appropriate student/sampling weights and replicate weights, and apply them when estimating uncertainty for country and subgroup comparisons.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study’s main outcomes are process-derived strategy indicators (similarity, consistency of similarity, efficiency, consistency of efficiency) computed from action sequences using the LCS method, rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. While the paper discusses excluding a specific nonresponse action-sequence pattern from the LCS analysis, it does not report a general missing-data handling procedure for the process indicators or the linked background variables beyond that exclusion rule. Therefore, missing-data handling is treated as not reported for the analytic pipeline.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper restricts the PIAAC sample to respondents who took the PS2 PSTRE module (seven PS2 items administered in the same order, no time limits). It further excludes respondents who had at least one occurrence of the shortest observable nonresponse sequence pattern (“Start, Next, Next_OK”) from the LCS analysis, resulting in 6,007 respondents used for reporting LCS results. The analysis is limited to five countries: England/N. Ireland (UK), Ireland, Japan, the Netherlands, and the United States, and it uses only the PS2 item cluster (PS1-PS2 routing paths are included in the PS2-taking sample).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PIAAC process data from the Problem Solving in Technology-Rich Environments (PSTRE) domain, focusing on the PS2 item cluster (seven interactive tasks) administered to adults routed to PS2 in five countries (England/N. Ireland (UK), Ireland, Japan, the Netherlands, United States). The study applies the longest common subsequence (LCS) sequence-mining approach to compare each respondent’s observed action sequence to expert-predefined reference sequences, producing indicators of similarity (mean LCS/reference overlap), consistency of similarity (standard deviation across items), efficiency (LCS/observed sequence overlap), and consistency of efficiency. Respondents with at least one nonresponse sequence pattern (“Start, Next, Next_OK”) are excluded from the LCS reporting sample (6,007). Results show that similarity varies significantly across countries (ANOVA), while consistency of similarity does not; similarity and consistency are associated with PSTRE proficiency level; and subgroup differences emerge by gender, age, and ICT familiarity. The report does not describe the use of PVs or a general missing-data handling strategy for the process indicators, and it does not incorporate action-timestamp information into efficiency.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD technical report focused on methodological development and descriptive/associational analysis of process-derived strategy indicators using LCS, rather than training predictive ML models with reported accuracy/AUC-type metrics. Consequently, the schema’s ML fields (primary/all_techniques) are left empty and main_findings is set to [] to avoid fabricating StructuredFinding rows. The report’s outcomes are strategy indicators and their relationships to proficiency and subgroup characteristics, which are analyzed with conventional statistical comparisons rather than supervised ML prediction.
